hints: Think about what a proton NMR spectrometer detects and compare the atoms present in $\text{CHCl}_{3}$ with those in $\text{CDCl}_{3}$.
walkthrough:
See what proton NMR actually sees**
Picture yourself as the spectrometer. You only respond to $^{1}\text{H}$ nuclei. Any proton in the sample, including protons in the solvent which is present in huge excess, will absorb and give a signal.

Compare the two solvents**
$\text{CHCl}_{3}$ has one $^{1}\text{H}$, so it would produce a large solvent peak that could hide peaks from compound E. In $\text{CDCl}_{3}$ that proton is replaced by deuterium, $^{2}\text{H}$ or D, which resonates at a completely different frequency and is invisible in a proton spectrum. That leaves the spectrum clean for E only.
Final answer: $\text{CDCl}_{3}$ contains no protons ($^{1}\text{H}$) so gives no peak in proton NMR, whereas $\text{CHCl}_{3}$ contains a proton and would give an interfering peak.

hints: Recall that chemical shift $\delta$ values are relative numbers in ppm, so think what is needed to fix the zero point of the scale.
walkthrough:
Fix the zero of the scale**
Chemical shift has no absolute value, it is always measured relative to something. TMS, $\text{Si}(\text{CH}_{3})_{4}$, is ideal because it has 12 equivalent protons in a highly shielded environment, giving one sharp singlet well away from most organic signals. Setting that singlet to $\delta = 0$ lets every other peak be quoted consistently.
Final answer: TMS is added as a standard / reference for measurement of chemical shift, set at $\delta = 0$.

hints: Focus on the evidence that hot $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ splits E into two organic products, one of which is the alcohol ethanol.
walkthrough:
Link ethanol to its parent functional group**
Hot aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ breaks an ester by alkaline hydrolysis: $\text{RCOOR}' + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{RCOONa} + \text{R}'\text{OH}$. The alcohol part $\text{R}'\text{OH}$ appears as a separate organic product. Here that alcohol is ethanol, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$, so the $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{O}$ fragment must have come from an ester group $\text{COOCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ in E.

hints: Recall the n+1 rule that a proton with n equivalent protons on the adjacent carbon is split into n+1 peaks.
Use the integration numbers 3 at $\delta = 1.4$ and 2 at $\delta = 4.3$ to work out which group is splitting which in a $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}$ fragment.
walkthrough:
Apply the n+1 rule**
Splitting comes from protons on the directly attached neighbouring carbon. If there are n equivalent neighbours, you see n+1 lines. This is spin-spin coupling, not coupling through oxygen or long range.

Decode the $\delta = 1.4$ triplet**
Integration 3 means a $\text{CH}_{3}$ group. It appears as three lines, a triplet, so n = 2. That tells you the adjacent carbon carries two protons, exactly what you expect for $\text{CH}_{3}$ next to $\text{CH}_{2}$ in $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{O}$.

Decode the $\delta = 4.3$ quartet**
Integration 2 means a $\text{CH}_{2}$ group. It appears as four lines, a quartet, so n = 3. That tells you the adjacent carbon carries three protons, exactly what you expect for $\text{CH}_{2}$ next to $\text{CH}_{3}$. Together the triplet plus quartet pair is the classic ethyl pattern, here deshielded to $\delta = 4.3$ by the attached oxygen of the ester.

Final answer: At $\delta = 1.4$: triplet, caused by two H on neighbouring C atom.
At $\delta = 4.3$: quartet, caused by three H on neighbouring C atom.

hints: Think which proton environment typically appears downfield between $\delta = 7.0$ and $8.5$ and can account for five protons together.
walkthrough:
Recognise the aromatic region**
Protons attached directly to a benzene ring are strongly deshielded by the ring current and appear around $\delta = 7$ to $8.5$. Five protons in that region with complex splitting fits a monosubstituted benzene, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}$, where the five ring protons are in slightly different environments but overlap.
Final answer: aryl group / phenyl group / benzene ring

hints: Combine the ester containing $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{O}$ from (c) and (d)(i) with the $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}$ group from (d)(ii) and check against $\text{C}_{9}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_{2}$.
walkthrough:
Assemble the whole molecule**
You have an ester with an ethyl alcohol part, $\text{COOCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, and a phenyl part, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}$. Joining them through the carbonyl gives $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COOCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$. Count atoms: $6+1+2 = 9$ carbons, $5+2+3 = 10$ hydrogens, 2 oxygens, matching $\text{C}_{9}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_{2}$. This is ethyl benzoate.

hints: For $m/e = 29$, calculate what hydrocarbon fragment from an ethyl group $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}$ would weigh.
For $m/e = 77$, calculate the mass of a $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}$ ring fragment after loss of the ester side chain.
walkthrough:
Assign $m/e = 29$**
In mass spectrometry $m/e$ for a singly charged ion equals its relative mass. $12 \times 2 + 1 \times 5 = 29$, so this is the ethyl cation from cleavage of the $\text{O-CH}_{2}$ bond: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}^{+}$.

Assign $m/e = 77$**
$12 \times 6 + 1 \times 5 = 77$, so this is the phenyl cation, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}^{+}$, formed by cleavage of the bond between the benzene ring and the carbonyl group. It is a very characteristic fragment for compounds containing a $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}$ group and strongly supports ethyl benzoate.

Final answer: fragment ion with $m/e = 29$: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}^{+} / \text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}^{+}$
fragment ion with $m/e = 77$: $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}^{+}$
